opus-5.5.text:
What excites me most is that it mirrors how biology is actually organized. Biology is hierarchical. Proteins interact with each other to form pathways and complexes, those give a cell its state and function, and then the cells, with their spatial arrangement and their interactions in a tissue, determine what's going on with the patient. For a long time we've modeled each of these levels in isolation. Some people build protein interaction networks, others do single-cell analysis, and on the clinical side people work with patient-level features. The exciting thing is that we can now build representations that flow information up the hierarchy in a principled way.

From a machine learning perspective, this is a natural fit for graph neural networks and hierarchical representation learning. You start with embeddings of proteins that capture their interaction context, their structure, and their function. Then you aggregate those into a cell representation, so a cell is described by which proteins are expressed and how they relate to each other, not just as a vector of gene counts. Then you aggregate cells into a patient, taking into account the composition of cell types, their states, and increasingly their spatial neighborhoods in the tissue. At every level you get a representation you can reason with, and they're all connected.

Scientifically, there are a few reasons this matters. The first is interpretability and mechanism. If a model predicts that a patient will respond to an immunotherapy, you want to know why. With a hierarchical model you can trace the prediction back down. It's being driven by this population of T cells in this spatial context, and within those cells by this particular set of proteins or pathways. That gives you hypotheses you can actually test in the lab, which is very different from a black-box score.

The second is generalization. Patient-level data is always scarce. You might have a few hundred patients in a cohort. But each patient has hundreds of thousands of cells, and each cell expresses thousands of proteins. By grounding the patient representation in these lower-level building blocks, which are shared across patients, diseases, and even datasets, you get a lot more statistical strength. The model learns what a dysfunctional T cell looks like once, and then it can recognize that in a new patient or a new disease.

The third, and maybe the most exciting long term, is that this moves us toward something like a virtual cell and eventually a virtual patient. If your representations are compositional, you can start asking counterfactual questions. What happens to this cell state if I knock down this protein? How does the patient's tissue composition shift if a drug targets this pathway? You can do perturbation reasoning at the molecular level and see how it propagates up to the patient outcome. That's where precision medicine really needs to go: not just stratifying patients, but understanding the mechanism well enough to design interventions.

And of course there are hard open problems, which is part of the fun. How do you aggregate in a way that doesn't wash out rare but important cell populations? How do you integrate different modalities, like transcriptomics, proteomics, and imaging, which measure different things at different resolutions? How do you handle batch effects across hospitals and technologies? But I think we finally have the data, with single-cell and spatial technologies, and the modeling tools, with graph learning and foundation models, to take this seriously. That combination is what makes it such an exciting moment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think what's really exciting here is that biology is fundamentally hierarchical, right? You have proteins that interact with each other, those interactions are happening inside cells, cells have different types and they live in different tissues, and then all of that together makes up a patient. And for the longest time, the way we've been doing machine learning in biomedicine has basically flattened all of that. You take a patient and you represent them as a bag of mutations, or a vector of gene expression values, and you throw away the structure.

And what I find exciting is that with graph neural networks, and more broadly with these multi-scale representation learning approaches, we actually have the tools now to respect that hierarchy. So you can start at the level of a protein, you can learn a representation of that protein based on its structure and its interactions in the protein-protein interaction network. Then you can say, okay, this protein is expressed in this particular cell type, in this particular tissue context, and you aggregate up. And the representation of the cell is now a function of the proteins that are active in it and how they interact. And then you go one level up and the patient becomes a function of what's happening across their cells and tissues.

The reason this matters scientifically is that the same protein can do very different things depending on the context. A mutation in a gene might be completely benign in one cell type and catastrophic in another. So if you don't model the context, you just can't capture that. And when you build the representation this way, from the bottom up, the model has a chance to actually learn those context-dependent effects rather than having us hand-engineer them.

The other thing I'd say is that it gives you a path toward something that looks like mechanistic interpretability for medicine. If a model tells you this patient is at high risk, you'd like to be able to trace that back, to say it's because of this cell type, driven by this pathway, driven by these proteins. When your representation is built hierarchically, that kind of explanation becomes much more natural, because the structure of the model mirrors the structure of the biology.

And honestly, from a pure machine learning perspective, I think it's a really interesting problem. How do you aggregate information across scales where the number of entities differs by orders of magnitude? You have tens of thousands of proteins, trillions of cells, and one patient. How do you do that in a way that's data efficient, given that we have far fewer patients than we'd like? Those are open questions, and I think they're some of the most fun ones to work on right now.

astra-6.text:
What I find scientifically exciting is that you’re connecting different levels of biological organization. At the molecular level, you have proteins and their interactions. Those interactions give rise to the behavior of cells, and then the cells, in their particular environments, contribute to what we observe in a patient.

The interesting question is how to build a representation that preserves those relationships. It’s not simply averaging all the proteins to get a cell and averaging all the cells to get a patient. Which proteins interact, which cells are present, and how those cells influence each other can all matter.

If we can capture that structure, then we have a way to connect a patient-level prediction back to a biological hypothesis. Why might two patients with the same diagnosis respond differently to treatment? Is there a particular cellular state or molecular pathway that could explain the difference? That connection between predicting an outcome and understanding the biology behind it is, to me, the really exciting scientific opportunity.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s exciting to me is that biology gives us a natural hierarchy, but we don’t yet know how to connect those levels computationally. Proteins interact with one another, those interactions determine what happens in a cell, and populations of cells contribute to the state of a patient. So the question is: how do we build a representation that captures those relationships across scales?

And aggregation here can’t just mean averaging everything together. The same protein can play a different role depending on the cell type or its environment. You want to preserve that context as you move from molecules to cells to the patient.

Scientifically, this creates an opportunity to connect molecular mechanisms with clinical outcomes. If two patients have similar representations, can we understand what biological processes make them similar? And if they respond differently to a treatment, can we trace that difference back to particular cells or pathways? That connection between predicting an outcome and understanding the biology behind it is what I find really exciting.
